newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada argues in Supreme Court: No UDI for Quebec.
newsitem.headline: Canada argues in Supreme Court: No UDI for Quebec.

text.p: The Canadian government argued in a controversial written submission to the Supreme Court on Friday that French-speaking Quebec has no right under domestic or international law to secede unilaterally.

Though it immediately drew the fury of Quebec separatists, the government was acting now to try to get a definitive verdict from the top court before the heat of another referendum, possible in the next few years.

Hard-line separatists, eager to have their own French country in a sea of North American English speakers, say neither the Supreme Court nor the Canadian constitution can legitimately limit their right to secede if they vote to do so.
Federal Justice Minister Allan Rock, meeting reporters after the submission, countered: "Those who demand democracy must embrace democratic institutions."

Canada came close to breaking up in October 1995 when 49.4 percent of Quebeckers voted in favor of sovereignty. Quebec's premier at the time, Jacques Parizeau, indicated afterwards that he had been prepared to move quickly toward independence if he got a Yes vote.

Rock said whatever the Supreme Court decides will make the situation clearer for Quebec residents, all Canadians and the rest of the world -- though he declined to say how this could be enforced if Quebec did try to leave on its own.
"I think any judgment they (the judges) come to will be respected here and abroad as authoritative," he said.
The argument echoed the position of Liberal Prime Minister Jean Chretien, that Quebeckers have a right to express their views in a referendum but that this would not be binding.

"The outcome of a referendum vote cannot, in and of itself, alter the basic constitutional principles and legal rules by which all Canadians are governed or the constitutional protections which they enjoy," the government said.

It said the constitution was capable of handling any change, including secession. The trouble with this argument, for those who advocate sovereignty, is that it could require approval of too many other provinces for this to realistically happen.
On the international plane, the government recognized a right to self-determination but said this right has never included a right to secede from democratic independent states.

"The principle of self-determination does not imply any right to unilateral secession from an independent state with a government representing its people on a basis of equality," the written argument said.
The official opposition in Parliament, the separatist Bloc Quebecois, blasted the submission as shameful.

"There isn't a Chretien on earth, there isn't a government, there aren't nine judges of the Supreme Court of Canada who are going to decide the future of the people of Quebec," Bloc Member of Parliament Michel Bellehumeur said.
"It is only the Quebec people who will decide that. It's purely a political question."
The separatist Quebec government has refused to take part in the court case, so the Supreme Court is likely to appoint lawyers to argue the separatist case.
Rock denied that hesitant people might vote for sovereignty just to send Ottawa a message if they thought Canada would not split up since the Canadian government would eventually block secession.
He said the question of any future referendum would be clear and the consequences would be made clear in advance.
Rock asked the Supreme Court to take up the case last September and a government official said the Supreme Court was most likely to hear oral arguments this autumn.
